title: Alignment patterns for inference buyers
content:
Purpose: Quick, pragmatic messaging + rebuttal + evidence set AEs and SEs can use when the buying group includes an ML engineer, a backend engineer, and a platform/infra lead. This is intentionally tactical: short lines to test in calls, plus competitor knockouts and two demo hooks (latency path and cost path).

Context and insight (problem statement):
- Buying group is often three personas with distinct priorities: ML engineers care about fidelity and model lifecycle; backend engineers care about latency, request patterns, and integration complexity; platform teams care about cost predictability, security, and operational controls.
- Conversations stall when the vendor pitches only one dimension (e.g., model accuracy) without mapping to operational cost/latency or rollout mechanics.

High-level positioning thesis (one sentence per persona):
- ML engineer: "Ship quality-first inference with versioning, reproducible evals, and rollback safety so you can iterate models without surprise regressions."
- Backend engineer: "Serve requests within your millisecond budget with predictable tail latency and simple SDKs that match your current stack."
- Platform lead: "Consolidate inference onto a single observable runtime that lets you control unit economics across teams and enforce security policies centrally."

Three talk-track patterns (short, testable lines):
1) The Latency Budget Frame (use with backend + platform):
   - Opening: "What's your tail latency SLA at 95/99? Where does that cause product friction today?"
   - Quick claim: "We route and fallback in-microseconds and maintain 99th percentile latencies via continuous batching+KV management; customers cut failed requests by X% vs naive autoscaling."
   - Evidence to pull: 95/99 latency charts from Console, plus a customer quote (internal: GT-412).
   - Demo hook: Warm KV cache demo — show 80% drop in median latency for repeated session tokens within 60s.

2) The Cost Staircase Frame (use with platform + backend):
   - Opening: "What does 1M inference tokens cost you today (infra + orchestration + ops time)?"
   - Quick claim: "We reduce per-token spend via batching, prefix caching, and quantization profiles; typical savings 20–60% depending on workload burstiness."
   - Evidence: Show Optimize recommendations, before/after runbooks, and a simple ROI calc: savings pay for reserved capacity in 2–3 months for medium workload.
   - Demo hook: Show a cost simulation comparing naive single-node autoscale vs Redwood Dedicated with recommended batching.

3) The Quality-Operationalized Frame (use with ML engineer):
   - Opening: "How are you tracking model quality over production prompts? Any automatic regression alerts tied to evals?"
   - Quick claim: "We tie prompt sets to model versions and surface regressions (semantic and token-level) with rollback and canary controls so you never push a silent drift into prod."
   - Evidence: Example of an eval regression alert and canary rollback timeline from a pilot customer.

Persona-specific scripts (copy-paste friendly):
- ML Engineer (30–60s):
  "We know iteration velocity matters — Redwood lets you version models and bind eval prompt sets to each version. That means if a new model underperforms on your critical prompts, you get an automated alert and can rollback or route traffic to the previous version in minutes. It keeps you focused on model improvements instead of firefighting production bugs."

- Backend Engineer (30–60s):
  "If your stack needs consistent millisecond budgets, you can pin model variants by latency profile, apply per-route batching, and use automatic fallback to cheaper variants under load. Integration is a REST/SDK call — we don't force a proxy or custom runtime in your app."

- Platform Lead (30–60s):
  "We centralize observability and enforce routing/cost policies across teams. You get token-level cost attribution, rollout controls (canary/A-B/auto-fallback), and a predictable reserved capacity option to avoid runaway cloud spend."

Common objections and short rebuttals (for quick use in discovery):
- "We already host models ourselves." -> "Totally reasonable — the hard part is optimizing inference economics and reliability at scale. Teams that self-host often end up maintaining custom batching/caching code and per-model tuning; Redwood abstracts that so your infra team can focus on core services, not per-model kernel engineering. We can run a 1-week pilot on non-sensitive traffic to show delta."
- "We can't send PII to a hosted vendor." -> "We support Private deployments (VPC / on-prem) and bring-your-own-KMS for keys; audit logs and per-request tracing are available. We can map your compliance checklist in the next call."
- "We're worried about vendor lock-in." -> "Our API is model-agnostic and supports model pinning and exportable inference artifacts. Policies and routing are declarative — you can migrate models or rollback without changing product code."

Competitive mapping (how to position vs common opponents):
- General cloud managed endpoints (big clouds):
  - Strengths to call out: deep infra and global regions.
  - Redwood counter: "We make inference economical across model variants and workloads via inference-aware batching and KV caching in the runtime — something generic endpoints don't tune automatically."
- Single-purpose LLM APIs:
  - Strengths: easy to call, simple pricing.
  - Redwood counter: "We trade a little setup for control — you get predictable capacity, observability, and rollout tooling geared for production apps."
- Self-hosted inference frameworks:
  - Strengths: customization and cost control (perceived).
  - Redwood counter: "We provide the runtime optimizations as a managed product or as a private deployable package; customers keep control without building and maintaining the orchestration and monitoring layer."

Demo checklist (what to show in a 20-minute technical demo):
1) Start: Quick topology slide (1 min).
2) Live Console: 95/99 latency chart + token-level cost breakdown (3 min).
3) Warm KV cache demo: Send session prompts showing latency drop (4 min).
4) Rollout demo: Promote model version, run canary, simulate regression, and show alert + rollback (6 min).
5) Cost sim: Run Optimize recommendation and show projected monthly savings (3–4 min).

Metrics to carry into conversations (short numbers to cite if available in collateral):
- Typical latency improvements for cached sessions: 40–80% lower median latency.
- Unit cost reduction via batching/prefix caching/quantization: 20–60% (workload-dependent).
- Onboarding time for a single inference route (hosted): < 1 day for a minimal POC.

Documented buyer questions to surface on discovery (use to split the room):
- ML engineer: "How do you validate a new model against our critical prompt sets?"
- Backend engineer: "What's your 99th percentile latency with 80 concurrent inferences at 512 tokens?"
- Platform lead: "How do you charge for reserved capacity and how granular is cost attribution?"

Sales play recommendations (2 quick plays):
- Play A (Quality-first pilot): Target ML engineer as owner; offer a 2-week pilot with eval hooks and one rollback drill. Win condition: observable regression alert + policy implemented.
- Play B (Economics-first migration): Target platform lead; run a cost simulation for a high-volume route and propose Dedicated capacity with 3-month commit. Win condition: committed pilot and shared cost baseline.

Open questions / research items (for PMs and field reps):
- Need up-to-date hard numbers for: average onboarding time across customer segments, median savings for batch-optimized chat workloads, and 95/99 latency baselines per model family to cite in playbooks.
- Collect two short customer quotes explicitly about rollback and about reserved-capacity ROI.

Next steps (owner: Sofia):
- Turn this into two one-pagers (AE quick scripts): 1) quality pilot, 2) cost migration. (Due: 2025-01-31)
- Pull concrete metric tiles from Console for the demo checklist and attach to the AE playbook.
- Validate objection language with Legal for private deployment claims.

Notes to self / informal:
- Keep language concrete and avoid buzzwords when talking to backend/platform — they want numbers and a simple migration plan.
- For ML engineers, lead with tooling that reduces risk (evals + rollback) rather than raw model accuracy claims.
